strings.name: Shinya Yamanaka
strings.role: Medical researcher · Pioneer of induced pluripotent stem cells
strings.summary: Shinya Yamanaka is a Japanese medical researcher who moved from orthopaedic practice into basic science. With his team he reprogrammed mature cells into induced pluripotent stem cells using a small set of transcription factors, first in mice and then humans. This expanded disease modelling, drug screening and regenerative medicine research. He shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Gurdon; these discoveries do not imply approval of a universal therapy. In 2026, image concerns about some coauthored papers prompted a case-by-case institutional response.
strings.coverageNote: Selected training, cellular reprogramming, institutional work and the 2026 response to image concerns; checked through November 2026. Experiments, manufacturing facilities and approved treatments are distinguished.
strings.influence.rationale: He advanced induced pluripotent stem cell research, changing the direction of cellular reprogramming, disease models and regenerative medicine.
strings.facts.fact-1.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-2.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-2.value: Medical degree, Kobe University, 1987; PhD, Osaka City University, 1993
strings.highlights.highlight-1.title: Induced pluripotent stem cells
strings.highlights.highlight-1.text: With his team, reported mouse iPS cells in 2006 and human iPS cells in 2007, demonstrating reprogramming of mature cells.
strings.highlights.highlight-2.title: Shared Nobel Prize
strings.highlights.highlight-2.text: Shared the 2012 medicine prize with John Gurdon for discovering that mature cells can be reprogrammed to pluripotency.
strings.timeline.event-1.title: Responds to concerns about paper images
strings.timeline.event-1.text: CiRA described corrections and continuing checks in individual papers, rejecting the conflation of different author roles and case outcomes into personal misconduct.
strings.timeline.event-2.title: Autologous iPS manufacturing facility opens
strings.timeline.event-2.text: The CiRA Foundation he leads established Y-FiT in Osaka for autologous cell manufacturing work; this was not general approval of a treatment.
strings.timeline.event-3.title: Becomes CiRA director emeritus
strings.timeline.event-3.text: Continued as professor and director emeritus after his directorship, while advancing cell supply and application research through the CiRA Foundation.
strings.timeline.event-4.title: Shares Nobel Prize with Gurdon
strings.timeline.event-4.text: Cellular reprogramming was recognized by the medicine prize, connecting Gurdon's earlier nuclear-transfer work with iPS cell research.
strings.timeline.event-5.title: CiRA is established
strings.timeline.event-5.text: Kyoto University established CiRA with him as director, building structures for basic research, cell stocks and clinical translation.
strings.timeline.event-6.title: Reports human iPS cells
strings.timeline.event-6.text: His team extended reprogramming to human somatic cells, creating new tools for patient-derived disease models and drug research.
strings.timeline.event-7.title: Reports mouse iPS cells
strings.timeline.event-7.text: With Kazutoshi Takahashi and other researchers, reprogrammed mouse somatic cells using four factors, establishing a basis for iPS cell technology.
strings.timeline.event-8.title: Earns doctorate and researches in the US
strings.timeline.event-8.text: After earning his Osaka City University doctorate, began postdoctoral work at Gladstone, deepening his move into molecular and cellular research.
strings.timeline.event-9.title: Graduates in medicine and enters practice
strings.timeline.event-9.text: Earned his medical degree at Kobe and undertook orthopaedic clinical training in Osaka before turning to basic research.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in Osaka
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Born in Osaka, Japan; later entered Kobe University's medical school, initially choosing a clinical career.
